newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka economy comes back year after bank bomb.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka economy comes back year after bank bomb.

text.p: The January 1996 bombing of Sri Lanka's Central Bank killed 100 people, shocked the world and dealt blows to some sectors, but it also showed the resilience in the country's economy, the Central Bank governor said.

Despite the suicide bomb that was designed to wreak economic havoc, Sri Lanka's GDP (gross domestic product) should grow by nearly four percent in 1996, governor A.S.Jayawardena told Reuters. In 1995, GDP grew by 5.5 percent.
Jayawardena said last year's growth is remarkable and is testimony to the dynamism of Sri Lanka's private sector.
Though 41 members of the Central Bank were killed and some 230 injured, vital operations such as clearing and market operations were up and running within the week.
"When faced with adversity, people come out in their best," said Jayawardena, who was also in the nine-story bank building at the time of the blast. He was not injured.
The building suffered massive damage when a supected Tamil separatist guerrilla rammed it with a lorry full of explosives.
The blast destroyed the heart of Colombo's financial district, which is now being rebuilt under a $400 million plan.
Damage to the Central Bank alone is estimated at about 1.5 billion rupees ($26.3 million), and is being met separately with help from the United States, Germany, China and Britain.
"Urban terrorism is something that Europeans, Americans and others dread. And the blast converted even middle-of-the-road countries to support the Sri Lankan government," he said.
Though day-to-day economic operations were kept running smoothly, parts of the economy were hit, especially tourism.
Central Bank figures showed tourist arrivals fell by 28 percent to 266,400 people in the first 11 months of 1996, compared to 371,000 in the same period in 1995.
The bombing also caused a dip in investor confidence and a fall in consumer spending, Jayawardena said.

Investor confidence in the manufacturing sector suffered most in 1996, with a substantial decline in implementation of approved projects, said Thilan Wijesinghe, Chairman of the Board of Investment (BOI), the government arm which facilitates local and foreign direct investment.
With tighter consumer spending, Sri Lanka's import growth also slowed.
Both officials, however, said the the economic slowdown in 1996 could not be blamed entirely on the January 31 bombing.
A severe drought during the monsoon season caused daily power cuts averaging five hours between March and August. This also contributed to the slowdown, they said.

Low investor confidence combined with the power cuts had an adverse impact on industry as a whole. Industrial exports grew by only 10.5 percent from January to November 1996, down from 14.9 percent in the same period in 1995.
Six months after the bank bombing, another bomb on a packed commuter train in a Colombo suburb on July 24 killed 57 people and further erroded confidence.

But the Sri Lankan capital, under a tight security blanket, has not been disturbed since and is seeing a gradual improvement in sentiment, with the war confined to remote areas in the country's north and east.

The Colombo Stock Exchange has been the first to respond to the improved sentiment. The all-share index has gained four percent in the first four weeks of 1997 on the back of good corporate growth expected this year.
Overall economic performance, which began improving towards the end of 1996, is expected to continue in 1997 and help the country to achieve GDP growth of at least 5.5 percent.
Jayawardena, a central banker for nearly 40 years, says he is happy 1996 is over. "1996 was the most difficult year because like the Phoenix, we had to rise from the ashes."
($=57 rupees)
